rv.q: Tom Stoppard's 'Arcadia' is arguably the finest play by a living dramatist, a work that manages to be simultaneously profound and entertaining, intellectually rigorous and emotionally satisfying.
This is as entertaining as it is enlightening, a rare combination that justifies the recent revival's move to Broadway.

This beguiling production of what Stoppard has called "a thriller and a romantic tragedy with jokes" is beautifully knit by Leveaux and led by some wonderful performances, including by Billy Crudup, Raul Esparza, Bel Powley and Lia Williams.

It may be Stoppard's best play, and even an indistinct production can't subdue its poignancy and wisdom.
On the plus side, Williams brings believability and ample humor to her role, and Riley is perfection.
Arcadia" is a play with marvelous potential to amuse, delight and inspire intellectual discussion late into the night, but this misjudged revival doesn’t really crack the equation.
Keeping the play's underlying emotions rather on the cool side, Leveaux grievously errs by usually pacing the conversations at a hasty clip.
